Each GPU maker has its own technology. Support varies by game and by card generation, so check which version your card can use.
good: In 2026, AI-based upscaling is mature and often looks close to native resolution. Treat frame-generated frame rates with care: they feel smoother but not more responsive.

short: The main chip in a phone, tablet or many laptops. It combines the CPU, graphics, AI unit, modem and more on one piece of silicon.
body: A system on a chip puts most of a computer onto a single chip. Besides the CPU cores, it contains the GPU, the NPU for AI tasks, the image processor for the camera and often the cellular modem.
Because everything is close together, it is fast and power-efficient. The SoC largely decides how quick a phone feels, how well it handles games and how good the photo processing is.
Phones with the same SoC can still perform differently, depending on cooling, software and how hard the maker lets the chip run.
good: In 2026, a flagship-class SoC from the last one or two years handles anything, including heavy games. Mid-range chips are smooth for everyday use; the gap shows in gaming and camera processing.

short: The manufacturing generation of a chip, named in nanometres, such as 3 nm. Smaller generally means more efficient, but the names are partly marketing.
body: Chip makers shrink transistors with each new generation. That fits more of them on a chip and lets them switch using less power, which helps speed and battery life.
The "3 nm" or "2 nm" label no longer measures any actual part of the transistor. It is a generation name, and different factories' "3 nm" processes are not identical.
The node is one factor among many. Chip design, cooling and software matter just as much to real-world performance.
good: In 2026, flagship phone and laptop chips are built on 3 nm-class processes, with the first 2 nm-class chips arriving. Mid-range chips often use 4–6 nm and are still efficient.

short: A screen technology that lets the refresh rate drop as low as 1 Hz when the image is still, saving battery while keeping 120 Hz for scrolling.
body: LTPO stands for low-temperature polycrystalline oxide. It is a type of backplane, the layer of transistors that controls each pixel in an OLED screen.
It can hold a static image with very little power, so the refresh rate can fall to 1–10 Hz. This makes high refresh rates and an always-on display much cheaper in battery terms.
Phones without LTPO can still switch between a few fixed rates, such as 60 and 120 Hz, but cannot go as low.
good: In 2026, LTPO is standard on flagship phones and smartwatches and is spreading into upper mid-range models and some tablets and laptops.

short: A way of dimming OLED screens by flickering them on and off very quickly. Some people get eye strain or headaches from low-frequency PWM.
body: Many OLED screens lower brightness by switching pixels on and off many times per second. The shorter the on-time, the dimmer the screen looks.
Most people do not notice. Sensitive people can experience eye strain, headaches or a feeling of flicker, especially at low brightness in dark rooms.
Higher PWM frequencies, such as 1,920 Hz or above, are easier on the eyes. Some phones offer DC-like dimming that lowers the current instead.
good: In 2026, many Android phones use high-frequency PWM of about 2,000–4,000 Hz or more. If you are sensitive to flicker, check reviews that measure PWM, or consider an LCD screen.

short: A zoom camera that folds light sideways with a prism, so a long lens fits inside a thin phone. It enables 3× to 10× optical zoom.
body: A normal phone camera points straight out of the back. A long zoom lens would not fit in the phone's depth.
A periscope camera uses a prism or mirror to bend light 90 degrees and run it along the phone's body. This allows a much longer lens and real optical zoom, typically around 5×.
Some designs move lens groups to offer continuous optical zoom between two levels. Combined with a high-resolution sensor, cropping gives good quality at in-between zoom levels.
good: In 2026, a periscope camera of about 3–5× with a 50 MP sensor is common on flagships and is spreading to upper mid-range phones. Look for OIS on the telephoto too.

short: The physical size of the light-sensitive chip in a camera. A bigger sensor captures more light, giving cleaner low-light photos and softer backgrounds.
body: Phone sensors are given in odd fractions like 1/1.3" or 1-inch type. A bigger number after the slash means a smaller sensor, and the "inch" value does not match a real measurement.
Sensor size matters more than megapixels. A larger sensor with fewer pixels often beats a tiny sensor with many.
In dedicated cameras, the common sizes are full-frame, APS-C and Micro Four Thirds. Even the smallest of these is much bigger than a phone sensor.
good: In 2026, flagship phones use main sensors of about 1/1.3" to 1-inch type. A 1/1.5" or bigger sensor is good for a mid-range phone; much smaller sensors struggle in low light.

short: A second camera with a very wide field of view, about 110–120 degrees, for landscapes, buildings and group shots in tight spaces.
body: An ultrawide camera fits much more into the frame than the main camera. It is great for architecture, interiors and dramatic perspectives.
It usually has a smaller sensor than the main camera, so it is weaker in low light. Edges can look stretched or soft.
Many ultrawide cameras have autofocus and double as a macro camera for close-up shots.
good: In 2026, a 50 MP ultrawide with autofocus is common on flagships. In budget phones, an 8 MP ultrawide is fine in daylight but weak indoors.

short: Lets a phone or watch send emergency messages via satellite when there is no mobile signal or Wi-Fi.
body: When you are out of range, the phone guides you to point it at a satellite and sends a short, compressed message to emergency services or a relay centre.
It works only outdoors with a clear view of the sky. Sending a message can take from seconds to minutes.
Coverage depends on the country and the provider. Some phones also offer satellite texting to contacts or, in some markets, basic data through partner networks.
good: In 2026, satellite SOS is available on many recent flagship phones and some smartwatches. Check that it works in your country and whether it is free or needs a plan.

short: How many years a maker promises to deliver system upgrades and security patches for a phone or tablet.
body: Updates fix security holes and bring new features. Once updates stop, a device becomes riskier to use for banking and personal data.
Policies differ: some promise a number of major OS upgrades, others a number of years of security patches. The count starts from the launch date, not from when you buy.
EU ecodesign rules in force since June 2025 require new phones and tablets sold in the EU to receive OS updates for at least five years after the model is no longer placed on the market.
good: In 2026, seven years of updates is the benchmark set by leading Android and iOS makers. Five years is acceptable; buy a model launched recently to get the most out of it.

short: A wireless charging standard with a magnetic ring that snaps the phone into the right spot. It charges at 15 W, or 25 W in its newer version.
body: The original Qi standard needed you to place the phone just right on the pad. Qi2 adds magnets based on Apple's MagSafe design, so the coils always line up.
Better alignment means faster, cooler and more efficient charging. It also allows magnetic accessories like car mounts, stands and wallets.
The newer Qi2 25 W version raises the top speed. Phones without built-in magnets can be "Qi2 Ready" and use a magnetic case.
good: In 2026, Qi2 is supported by recent iPhones and a growing number of Android phones. Look for Qi2 25 W chargers and certified products for the best speed and safety.

short: Apple's magnetic wireless charging and accessory system for iPhone. Recent models charge at up to 25 W with a compatible charger.
body: MagSafe puts a ring of magnets around the charging coil in the iPhone. Chargers, cases, wallets and mounts snap on in the right place.
The magnetic design became the basis of the Qi2 standard, so many Qi2 chargers work with iPhones too.
The fastest speeds need a recent iPhone, a matching charger and a strong enough power adapter.
good: In 2026, MagSafe and Qi2 25 W chargers are interchangeable for most recent iPhones. Pick certified accessories and check the required adapter wattage.

short: A phone with a flexible screen that folds in half. Book-style models open into a small tablet; flip-style models fold into a compact square.
body: Book-style foldables open to a screen of about 7–8 inches, great for reading, multitasking and video. Flip models fold a normal-size phone in half to fit small pockets.
The inner screen uses a flexible OLED with a plastic or ultra-thin glass top layer. It is softer than a normal phone screen, and a faint crease along the hinge is common.
Recent foldables are thinner and lighter and often have IP48 or better water resistance, though dust protection is still limited.
good: In 2026, foldables are much more durable than early models. Check hinge warranty, dust rating, repair costs and whether the camera matches non-folding flagships.

short: A short-range radio technology that measures distance and direction very precisely. Used to find item trackers, unlock cars and share files.
body: UWB sends very short pulses over a wide frequency range. By timing them, two devices can work out their distance to within centimetres, plus the direction.
This enables precise item-tracker finding with on-screen arrows, digital car keys that unlock as you approach, and pointing a phone at another device to share.
It complements Bluetooth and NFC rather than replacing them.
good: In 2026, UWB is common on flagship phones and smartwatches. It is a nice extra if you use trackers or a digital car key; most people will not miss it.

short: A mode that keeps the time, notifications and other basics visible on a dimmed screen while the device is idle.
body: On OLED screens, black pixels are switched off, so showing a few lit elements uses little power. That makes an always-on display practical.
On phones it typically costs a few percent of battery a day. On smartwatches the cost is higher relative to the small battery, often cutting battery life noticeably.
LTPO screens that drop to 1 Hz make always-on displays more efficient.
good: In 2026, AOD is standard on most OLED phones and smartwatches. On a watch, expect battery life to drop with AOD on; check reviews for the real figure.

short: An OLED panel type that adds a quantum dot layer to create colours. It gives very bright, saturated colours with perfect blacks.
body: Standard WOLED panels use white OLED light with colour filters. QD-OLED uses blue OLED light and converts part of it into red and green with quantum dots.
This gives purer colours at high brightness and wide viewing angles. Like all OLED, each pixel lights itself, so blacks are perfect and response is near instant.
In bright rooms, some QD-OLED panels look slightly grey when off because of the lack of a polariser. Newer generations have reduced this effect.
good: In 2026, QD-OLED and modern WOLED both deliver top picture quality. For monitors, QD-OLED is a leading choice for gaming; compare peak brightness and burn-in warranties.

short: Separately controlled areas of an LCD backlight. More zones give deeper blacks and less glow around bright objects.
body: An LCD screen needs a backlight. With local dimming, the backlight is split into zones that can be brightened or dimmed independently to match the picture.
Mini-LED TVs and monitors can have hundreds or thousands of zones. Fewer zones can cause blooming, a halo of light around bright objects on a dark background.
Edge-lit dimming uses lights along the sides and is much less effective than a full-array backlight behind the screen.
good: In 2026, a good mini-LED TV has hundreds to a few thousand zones, and good HDR monitors 500 or more. The processing behind the zones matters as much as the count.

short: Two HDMI 2.1 gaming features. VRR matches the screen's refresh rate to the game; ALLM switches the TV to game mode automatically.
body: VRR (variable refresh rate) lets the TV refresh exactly when a new frame arrives from the console or PC. This removes tearing and reduces stutter when the frame rate dips.
ALLM (auto low latency mode) tells the TV to switch to its game mode when a game starts and back when you watch a film. That keeps input lag low without fiddling with settings.
Both are part of HDMI 2.1. FreeSync and G-Sync are related VRR technologies, mainly used on PCs and monitors.
good: In 2026, a gaming TV should have VRR across the full 48–120 Hz range (or 144 Hz) and ALLM on at least two HDMI 2.1 ports.

short: An HDR format that adds scene-by-scene brightness information, so a TV can adjust its picture more precisely. A royalty-free rival to Dolby Vision.
body: Basic HDR10 uses one set of brightness information for a whole film. HDR10+ adds dynamic metadata that changes scene by scene.
This helps TVs that cannot reach the full brightness of the master to tone-map each scene sensibly, keeping detail in highlights and shadows.
Some streaming services and Blu-ray discs use HDR10+, others Dolby Vision, and some both. A newer HDR10+ Advanced version adds further features.
good: In 2026, the ideal TV supports HDR10, HDR10+ and Dolby Vision. If one is missing, the TV falls back to basic HDR10, which still looks good on a capable set.

short: A VESA test standard for HDR monitors and laptops. The number, such as DisplayHDR 600, shows the minimum peak brightness in nits.
body: Many monitors claim HDR support without being bright enough to show it properly. DisplayHDR sets testable minimums for brightness, black level, colour and dimming.
The tiers are 400, 500, 600, 1000 and 1400, plus True Black 400, 500 and 600 for OLED screens. True Black tiers focus on deep blacks rather than very high brightness.
DisplayHDR 400 is a low bar: it often lacks real local dimming and looks only a little better than SDR.
good: In 2026, DisplayHDR 600 or higher, or any True Black tier, gives a real HDR experience. Treat DisplayHDR 400 as basic.

short: A colour range used for cinema and HDR content that is about 25% larger than sRGB. Coverage is given as a percentage.
body: DCI-P3 was made for digital cinema and is now the reference for HDR video and many phone screens. It includes richer reds and greens than sRGB.
A screen with 95% DCI-P3 coverage can show almost all of those colours. A wider gamut makes HDR content look more vivid.
For office work and the web, sRGB accuracy matters more. A wide-gamut screen without a proper sRGB mode can make normal content look oversaturated.
good: In 2026, about 95% DCI-P3 or more is typical for OLED and good mini-LED screens. For editing, also check factory calibration and an accurate sRGB mode.

short: A monitor much wider than standard 16:9, giving more horizontal space for multitasking, editing timelines and immersive games.
body: A 21:9 monitor is about one third wider than a 16:9 screen of the same height. Common sizes are 34 inches at 3440 × 1440. Super ultrawide 32:9 screens equal two 16:9 monitors side by side.
They replace a two-monitor setup without a gap in the middle. Most are curved to keep the edges at a comfortable viewing angle.
Not all games and videos support these shapes; you may see black bars. They also need a stronger graphics card than a 16:9 monitor of the same height.
good: In 2026, a 34-inch 3440 × 1440 ultrawide at 144 Hz or more is the popular sweet spot. OLED ultrawides offer the best picture; check text clarity if you work with documents.

short: A monitor that connects to a laptop with one USB-C cable carrying video, data and charging power.
body: With a USB-C or Thunderbolt monitor, one cable shows the picture, links the monitor's USB ports and charges the laptop at the same time.
The power rating, such as 65 W or 90 W, shows how much it can deliver. If it is less than your laptop needs, the battery may drain slowly under heavy load.
Many such monitors also have a built-in KVM switch and Ethernet port, which turns them into a simple dock.
good: In 2026, 65 W is enough for most thin laptops; 90–100 W suits larger ones. Check that your laptop's USB-C port supports video (DisplayPort Alt Mode).

short: A surround sound format that adds height to sound, so effects can seem to come from above as well as around you.
body: Classic surround sound sends audio to fixed channels, such as 5.1. Atmos places sounds as objects in 3D space, and the system works out which speakers should play them.
Full setups use ceiling or upward-firing speakers. Soundbars and TVs simulate height with angled drivers or processing, with mixed results.
Headphones can render Atmos as spatial audio. Streaming services, Blu-rays and many games offer Atmos tracks.
good: In 2026, Atmos support is common in mid-range and better soundbars and TVs. For a real height effect, look for upward-firing drivers or separate height speakers.

short: The newer Bluetooth audio standard. It uses the efficient LC3 codec and adds Auracast, which lets one device stream to many headphones at once.
body: LE Audio is built on Bluetooth Low Energy. Its LC3 codec sounds better than the old SBC codec at the same bitrate, so it can save battery or improve quality.
Auracast is a broadcast feature. A phone, TV or public venue can send audio to any number of nearby compatible headphones, speakers or hearing aids, for example to share music or listen to a gym TV.
LE Audio also improves support for hearing aids and allows true stereo with lower latency. Both the source and the headphones must support it.
good: In 2026, LE Audio and Auracast are supported by many new phones, earbuds and hearing aids, but not yet everywhere. It is a good future-proof feature rather than a must-have.

short: Processing that makes headphone sound seem to come from around you, like speakers in a room. Head tracking keeps it fixed as you turn.
body: Normal stereo sounds as if it is inside your head. Spatial audio uses filters based on how ears hear direction, placing sounds in front, around and above you.
With head tracking, sensors in the earbuds detect head movement so the sound stays anchored to the screen or room.
It works best with surround or Atmos mixes. With regular stereo music, many people prefer it off. Some systems personalise it with a scan of your ears.
good: In 2026, spatial audio with head tracking is standard on flagship earbuds and headphones. It works best within the same brand's phone and earbuds.

short: A headphone mode that uses the microphones to let outside sound in, so you can hear announcements, traffic or a conversation without removing them.
body: Noise-cancelling earbuds and headphones block a lot of outside sound. Transparency mode does the opposite: the microphones pick up your surroundings and play them through the speakers.
Good transparency sounds natural, as if you were not wearing anything. Weaker versions sound hissy or artificial.
Adaptive modes now blend noise cancelling and transparency automatically, reducing loud sounds while keeping voices clear.
good: In 2026, transparency mode is expected on any earbuds with ANC. Natural-sounding transparency and an adaptive mode are signs of a well-made model.

short: The range of pitches a speaker or headphone can play, such as 20 Hz–20 kHz. The range alone says little about how good it sounds.
body: Human hearing covers roughly 20 Hz (deep bass) to 20 kHz (high treble), and the upper limit drops with age. Most headphones claim at least this range.
What matters more is how even the response is across that range, and how it is tuned. A graph from an independent measurement tells you far more than two numbers.
For speakers, the lower limit is useful: it shows how deep the bass goes. Small portable speakers often stop around 60–80 Hz.
good: In 2026, nearly all headphones list 20 Hz–20 kHz or wider. Use reviews with measurements to judge sound. For speakers, a low limit of 50 Hz or below means solid bass.

short: The delay between a sound being played on the device and reaching your ears through wireless headphones, in milliseconds.
body: Bluetooth audio has to be compressed, sent and decoded, which takes time. Typical delays are 100–250 ms.
Video apps hide this by delaying the picture, so lips stay in sync. Games and music apps cannot do that, so you may notice sounds arriving late.
Gaming modes, LE Audio and dedicated 2.4 GHz wireless dongles cut latency to roughly 20–80 ms. Wired headphones have essentially none.
good: In 2026, a gaming or low-latency mode under about 80 ms is good for casual games. For competitive gaming, use a 2.4 GHz dongle or a wired connection.

short: Digital audio with more detail than CD quality, usually 24-bit at 96 kHz or higher. A label also used on headphones and speakers that can play it.
body: CD quality is 16-bit at 44.1 kHz. Hi-res audio files use 24-bit and sample rates of 48, 96 or 192 kHz.
Many streaming services offer lossless and hi-res tracks. Whether you can hear a difference depends on your equipment, ears and the recording.
Over Bluetooth, full hi-res does not get through. Codecs such as LDAC or aptX Lossless carry more data than standard ones, but wired is still the only way to hear the file as it is.
good: In 2026, lossless streaming is widely available. Good headphones and a well-mastered recording matter far more than the sample rate on the label.

short: Earbuds that rest outside or beside the ear canal, leaving it open so you hear your surroundings. Includes air-conduction and bone-conduction types.
body: Open-ear models hook over or clip onto the ear and point sound into it without sealing it. Bone-conduction models send vibrations through the cheekbones instead.
Because your ears stay open, you hear traffic and people around you. That makes them popular for running, cycling and office use. They are also comfortable for long periods.
They cannot block noise and have weaker bass than sealed earbuds. Sound can leak to people nearby at high volume.
good: In 2026, open-ear earbuds are a big, well-developed category. Pick them for sport and awareness, not for noisy commutes or flights.

short: Numbers that describe a sound system: main channels, then subwoofers, then height channels. 5.1.2 means five main, one sub and two height channels.
body: The first number counts speakers around you at ear level: left, centre, right, sides and rear. The second counts subwoofers for deep bass.
A third number, used with Dolby Atmos and similar formats, counts height channels from the ceiling or upward-firing drivers.
Soundbars quote these numbers for virtual channels too. A soundbar with real rear speakers usually sounds more convincing than one that relies on processing alone.
good: In 2026, a 3.1 soundbar with a clear centre channel greatly improves TV speech. For true surround, look for 5.1.2 or better with real rear and upward-firing speakers.

term: Full-frame, APS-C and Micro Four Thirds
short: The main sensor sizes in interchangeable-lens cameras. Full-frame is largest, APS-C is about 1.5× smaller, Micro Four Thirds smaller again.
body: A full-frame sensor is about 36 × 24 mm, the size of a 35 mm film frame. APS-C is about 23 × 15 mm and Micro Four Thirds about 17 × 13 mm.
Larger sensors gather more light, which helps in low light and makes it easier to blur the background. Smaller sensors allow smaller, lighter and cheaper lenses.
Smaller sensors also "crop" the image. A 50 mm lens on APS-C frames like about 75–80 mm on full-frame.
good: In 2026, APS-C is the best value for most enthusiasts and travel, full-frame for low light and professional work, and Micro Four Thirds for compact kits and video.

short: A camera with interchangeable lenses but no mirror inside. You see the image on an electronic viewfinder or screen, straight from the sensor.
body: DSLR cameras use a mirror to bounce light up into an optical viewfinder. Mirrorless cameras remove it, so the sensor is always live.
This makes them smaller and allows advanced autofocus that tracks eyes, faces, animals and vehicles across the frame. What you see in the viewfinder matches the final exposure.
Major brands have moved their new development to mirrorless systems; new DSLR models are now rare.
good: In 2026, a mirrorless camera is the default choice for anyone buying a new interchangeable-lens system. Check lens choice, battery life and stabilisation alongside the body.

short: Stabilisation built into the camera body that moves the sensor to counter shake. It works with any lens you attach.
body: Lens-based stabilisation (OIS) moves elements inside the lens. IBIS moves the sensor itself on several axes, so even old or unstabilised lenses benefit.
Many cameras combine both systems for the best results. Ratings are given in stops: 5 stops means you can use a shutter speed about 32 times slower without blur.
IBIS helps with still subjects and handheld video. It cannot freeze a moving subject; that still needs a fast shutter speed.
good: In 2026, IBIS of about 5–8 stops is common in mid-range and better mirrorless cameras. It is very useful for low-light photos and handheld video.

short: How much a camera amplifies the signal from the sensor. Higher ISO allows shooting in darker places, but adds noise.
body: ISO 100 is used in bright light and gives the cleanest image. Raising ISO to 1,600, 6,400 or higher brightens the picture without a slower shutter or wider aperture.
The cost is noise: grain and blotchy colour, especially in shadows. Larger sensors handle high ISO better.
Maximum ISO figures like 102,400 are mostly marketing. What matters is the highest ISO you find acceptable for your use.
good: In 2026, modern full-frame cameras give clean results up to about ISO 6,400–12,800, APS-C about one stop less. Phones use multi-frame processing to cope with low light instead.

short: A small high-resolution screen inside the camera eyepiece that shows exactly what the sensor sees, including exposure and focus aids.
body: An EVF shows a live preview of the final image, so you see brightness, colour and depth of field before you press the shutter.
It can overlay helpful tools such as a histogram, focus peaking and a level. Compared with an optical viewfinder, it can lag slightly or flicker in very dark scenes, though modern ones are fast.
Resolution is given in dots: a higher count gives a sharper view. Magnification and refresh rate also matter.
good: In 2026, about 3.69 million dots is good for mid-range cameras, with 5.76 million or more in high-end models. A 120 Hz refresh helps when following action.

short: Video recorded with more colour levels (10-bit) and a flat log profile, giving more room to adjust colour and brightness when editing.
body: Standard 8-bit video stores 256 levels per colour. 10-bit stores 1,024, so skies and gradients stay smooth after editing.
Log profiles record a flat, low-contrast image that keeps more detail in highlights and shadows. It looks dull straight out of the camera and needs colour grading.
Many phones and cameras now offer 10-bit log or HDR video. Files are larger and need a capable editor and computer.
good: In 2026, 10-bit recording is standard on mid-range cameras and flagship phones. Use log only if you plan to colour-grade; otherwise standard or HDR profiles are easier.

short: GPS that receives two satellite frequencies (L1 and L5) instead of one. It gives more accurate tracks in cities, forests and mountains.
body: Single-band GPS can be thrown off by signals bouncing off tall buildings or cliffs. That causes jumpy routes and wrong distances.
Dual-band receivers listen on two frequencies and compare them, which filters out much of the error. Using several satellite systems at once also helps.
It uses a bit more battery. Many watches let you choose dual-band only for activities where accuracy matters.
good: In 2026, dual-band GPS is standard on sports watches and many premium smartwatches. It is worth having if you run, hike or cycle in cities or rough terrain.

short: A sensor that estimates the percentage of oxygen in your blood using light. Watches use it mainly for sleep and altitude insights.
body: The watch shines red and infrared light into the skin and measures how much is absorbed. Oxygen-rich blood absorbs light differently from oxygen-poor blood.
Healthy readings are usually 95–100% at rest. Watches can spot trends, such as dips during sleep or at high altitude.
Wrist readings are less reliable than a fingertip oximeter. Skin tone, fit, movement and cold hands can affect accuracy. It is not a medical diagnosis.
good: In 2026, SpO2 is common on mid-range and better smartwatches. Treat it as a wellness trend; see a doctor if you have breathing problems.

short: An electrical heart-rhythm reading taken by touching the watch's crown or bezel. It can flag signs of atrial fibrillation (AFib).
body: A smartwatch ECG records a single-lead electrocardiogram over about 30 seconds. You touch the watch with a finger from the other hand to close the circuit.
Cleared versions can classify the result as normal sinus rhythm or possible AFib, a common irregular rhythm that raises stroke risk.
It is not a full 12-lead hospital ECG and cannot detect heart attacks. Availability depends on regulatory approval in each country.
good: In 2026, ECG is standard on many premium smartwatches. Check that the feature is approved and enabled in your country before buying for it.

short: Green LEDs and light sensors on the back of a watch or band that track your pulse by measuring blood flow under the skin.
body: With each heartbeat, the amount of blood in the wrist changes slightly. The sensor detects this through changes in reflected light.
It works well at rest and for steady exercise. Fast changes, such as interval training or weightlifting, and a loose strap reduce accuracy.
For the most accurate readings during sport, a chest strap is still better. Many watches can pair with one.
good: In 2026, multi-LED sensors are standard and accurate for daily use. For serious training, look for a watch that accepts external chest straps.

short: USB Power Delivery is the main fast-charging standard for USB-C. PPS adds fine voltage steps that some phones need for their top charging speed.
body: USB PD lets a charger and device agree on voltage and current, from 5 V up to 20 V, or 48 V in the newest version. It powers phones, tablets and laptops.
PPS (programmable power supply) is an option within USB PD. The voltage can be adjusted in small steps, which reduces heat in the phone and allows faster charging.
Many Android phones reach their highest advertised speed only with a PPS charger. Look for "PPS" and the supported voltage range on the label.
good: In 2026, a good power bank or charger supports USB PD 3.x with PPS. 20–30 W covers phones, 45–65 W is good for tablets and small laptops, and 100 W or more for larger laptops.

short: Lets a power bank charge your devices while it is itself plugged in and charging, so you can use one wall socket for both.
body: With pass-through, you plug the power bank into the wall and your phone into the power bank. Both get charged, usually with priority on the connected device.
It is convenient when travelling with few sockets. Some power banks briefly cut output when the wall charger is plugged in or removed.
Frequent pass-through use can make a power bank warmer, which ages the battery. Quality models manage this better.
good: In 2026, pass-through is common on mid-range power banks. Check that output does not cut out during switching if you use it with devices that are sensitive to interruptions.

term: Power bank real capacity (mAh vs Wh)
short: The mAh on a power bank refers to its internal battery cells. Real output to your phone is typically about 60–70% of that figure.
body: A "20,000 mAh" rating is measured at the cell voltage of about 3.7 V. That is roughly 74 Wh of stored energy.
Converting to USB voltages and charging your device loses energy as heat. So a 20,000 mAh power bank will usually refill a 5,000 mAh phone about two and a half times, not four.
Watt-hours (Wh) are the fairer number. Airlines also use Wh: power banks up to 100 Wh can go in hand luggage, 100–160 Wh need approval, and they are not allowed in checked bags.
good: In 2026, 10,000 mAh suits daily phone top-ups and 20,000 mAh trips or tablets. Check Wh for flying; a growing number of airlines restrict using power banks during flights.

short: A standard measure of projector brightness. Unlike "LED lumens" or "light source lumens", ANSI lumens can be compared between brands.
body: ANSI lumens are measured in a set way: the average brightness at several points of a white screen. The newer ISO 21118 lumens are measured in a similar way.
Some makers quote inflated figures such as "LED lumens" or light source lumens, which can be several times higher than the real image brightness.
Brighter projectors cope better with ambient light and larger screens. In a dark room, contrast matters more than extra lumens.
good: In 2026, about 1,500–2,500 ANSI lumens is fine for a darkened living room, 3,000 or more for rooms with some light. Be wary of budget models with no ANSI figure.

short: The distance from projector to screen divided by the image width. A 1.5:1 ratio means you stand 1.5 m back for each metre of picture width.
body: Throw ratio tells you how big a picture you get from a given distance. For a 2.2 m wide image at 1.5:1, the projector must be about 3.3 m from the screen.
Short-throw projectors (below about 1:1) create a big picture from close up. Ultra-short-throw models (below about 0.4:1) sit just centimetres from the wall.
A zoom lens gives a range of ratios, which makes placement easier. Lens shift lets you move the image up or down without tilting the projector.
good: In 2026, check the throw ratio against your room before buying. Ultra-short-throw laser models are popular as TV replacements but need a special ambient light rejecting screen to look their best.

term: Laser vs lamp vs LED projector
short: The light source inside a projector. Lamps are cheap but fade and need replacing; LED and laser last for many years and start instantly.
body: Traditional lamp projectors give a bright image at a low price. The lamp dims over time and needs replacing after a few thousand hours.
LED projectors last much longer and are compact, but are usually less bright. Laser projectors combine high brightness with a lifespan of 20,000 hours or more.
Laser and LED switch on and off instantly and keep their colour and brightness more steadily. They cost more at the start.
good: In 2026, laser is the mainstream choice for living-room projectors, LED for small portable ones. Lamp models still make sense for tight budgets and occasional use.

short: How strongly a vacuum cleaner pulls in air, given in pascals (Pa) for robots or air watts (AW) for cordless models. Figures are not standardised.
body: Pascals measure the pressure difference the motor creates. Air watts combine pressure and airflow. Both give a rough idea of pulling power.
Makers test in their own way, so figures between brands are hard to compare. Brush design, sealing and airflow often matter more than the peak number.
Peak suction is usually only on the highest mode, which also drains the battery fastest.
good: In 2026, mid-range robot vacuums claim about 8,000–12,000 Pa, flagships 20,000 Pa or more. Cordless stick vacuums of about 150–250 AW cope well with carpets. Rely on cleaning tests.

short: A spinning laser sensor that maps rooms so a robot vacuum cleans in neat lines, knows where it is and avoids missing areas.
body: LiDAR measures distances by bouncing laser light off walls and furniture. The robot builds a precise floor map and cleans room by room.
With a map, you can set no-go zones, clean specific rooms and schedule tasks in the app. LiDAR also works in the dark, unlike camera-only navigation.
Front cameras or 3D sensors are often added to recognise and avoid small objects such as cables, socks and pet mess.
good: In 2026, LiDAR is standard on mid-range robots and above. Look for it combined with front obstacle avoidance; some newer models hide the laser to fit under low furniture.

short: A dock that sucks dirt out of the robot vacuum into a larger bag, so you only empty it every few weeks.
body: After each run, the robot returns to its dock, which empties the small onboard bin into a bag of about 2.5–4 litres.
All-in-one stations also refill and wash mop pads, dry them with warm air and refill a clean water tank.
Emptying is loud for a few seconds. Bags are an ongoing cost, and stations take up floor space.
good: In 2026, a self-emptying dock with about 6–8 weeks of capacity is common from the mid-range up. For hard floors, a full station with mop washing and hot-air drying saves the most work.
